title: Bright's fifth opinion is confuted
pass_a_gloss:
Article XIV. The fifth opinion, which is that of Timothy Bright of Cambridge, is confuted.
1. When I was putting the last hand to this disputation, the book of the most acute Timothy Bright of Cambridge On Health, On Disease, and On Death fell into my hands; in which he proposes a new and unaccustomed opinion on the origin of the soul. His words are these: To which we answer that neither the whole nor a part of the parents' mind is translated, nor is some accident a rudiment of the mind. What then? Surely a certain substance born from the soul — neither the whole itself nor a part — as an immortal seed of the soul, a principle of the offspring's future soul: and just as corporeal seed cut off from the parents' bodies emits neither the body itself nor some member of the body, so the soul is translated into the offspring through a fertile seed of the soul, not through the soul or some part of the soul: and a little later, Therefore we hold that the soul as integral and complete is to be referred as received to the parents; but something seminal shut out from the soul equally as from the body, and at length by the virtue of that word (namely the blessing of fertility) to go forth into a rational and immortal soul.
2. I confute this opinion of the most illustrious and learned Timothy thus. First: That spirit or spiritual seed which is shut out and emitted from the parent's soul truly and really pre-existed in the soul: for real emission presupposes real inherence; but that spirit cannot really inhere in the parent's soul: Therefore neither can it really be shut out and emitted from it. The assumption is proved: that spirit cannot inhere in the father's soul as a part in a whole, as Timothy himself admits; nor as an accident in a subject, because it is a substance, and it is repugnant to a substance to inhere in a subject; nor as a thing in a surrounding place or in a containing vessel — for such a mode of containment and circumscription is repugnant to the spiritual nature of the soul.
3. Second: that spiritual seed either comes to be from the whole father's soul, or from a part of the father's soul, or from nothing: for it cannot come to be from corporeal matter, both because it is a spiritual substance and because Bright himself testifies that it was born not from the body but from the soul: it does not come to be from the whole father's soul, because then the whole father's soul would be converted into seed; nor from a part, because the soul is indivisible; Therefore from nothing — which imports creation.
4. Third: the conversion of that spiritual seed into a soul is either an accidental conversion, such as the conversion or change by which a bad human is converted and changed into a good one, and white color into black; or it is a substantial conversion, such as was the conversion of Lot's wife into a pillar of salt, and the conversion of wood into the substance of that fire to which it is brought near. It is not an accidental conversion, because from that it would follow that that spiritual seed does not differ in species and essentially, but by a degree of accidental perfection, from the soul — that is, that it is a rational soul begun and imperfect by some accidental reason: but this contradicts Timothy's own words, saying that seed is not actually a soul but a principle of a future soul. But if it is a substantial conversion, then it happens either by abolition of the whole, or by abolition of one part of the essence with the other remaining.
5. Fourth: God could annihilate that seed and, it being annihilated, produce a soul from nothing in the same instant; then the production of the soul is to be ascribed not to the father but to God alone — which is a huge absurdity if their doctrine of the translate is true.
6. Fifth: conversion of seed into soul cannot happen by abolition of one part of the essence with the other remaining: first, because from that it would follow that that spiritual substance of the seed is corruptible and capable of substantial transmutation no less than physical bodies; for those can be abolished and destroyed naturally as to one sole part of the essence, namely the form: second, it would follow that that spiritual substance is composed of physical matter and form, or into essential parts — for of these alone is it true that when one of them is destroyed the other can remain surviving as to actual existence.
7. Sixth: generation of a human cannot happen without the perishing of the seed if that spiritual seed is converted into a soul; for the form of the seed, i.e. the soul, would remain — but substantial conversion requires the perishing of the prior form. Whence I conclude that Bright's opinion is no safer than the preceding ones.
pass_b_english: Article XIV. Bright's fifth opinion is confuted.

1. As I was finishing this disputation, Timothy Bright of Cambridge's On Health, Disease, and Death came to hand, with a new opinion on the soul's origin. He answers: neither the whole nor a part of the parents' mind is translated, nor is some accident a mind-rudiment. What then? A substance born from the soul — neither whole nor part — as an immortal seed of the soul, principle of the offspring's future soul. As corporeal seed cut from the parents' bodies is neither the body nor a member, so the soul is translated through a fertile soul-seed, not through the soul or a part of it. The integral soul is referred to the parents as received; but something seminal is shut out from soul as from body, and by the blessing of fertility goes forth into a rational immortal soul.

2. First confutation: that spiritual seed truly pre-existed in the parent's soul — real emission presupposes real inherence — yet it cannot really inhere there, so cannot be really emitted. Not as part in whole (Bright admits); not as accident in a subject (it is a substance); not as in a surrounding place or vessel (repugnant to the soul's spiritual nature).

3. Second: the spiritual seed comes from the whole father's soul, or a part, or nothing. Not from corporeal matter — it is spiritual, and Bright says it is born from soul not body. Not from the whole soul (the whole would convert into seed); not from a part (the soul is indivisible). So from nothing — which is creation.

4. Third: conversion of that seed into a soul is accidental or substantial. Not accidental: then it would differ from the soul only by degree of accidental perfection — an inchoate imperfect rational soul — contradicting Bright's claim that it is not actually a soul but a principle of a future soul. If substantial, it happens by abolishing the whole, or one part of the essence while the other remains.

5. Fourth: God could annihilate that seed and in the same instant produce a soul from nothing; then production belongs to God alone, not the father — a huge absurdity if their traducian doctrine is true.

6. Fifth: conversion cannot abolish one essential part while another remains. That would make the spiritual seed-substance corruptible and capable of substantial change like physical bodies; and would make it composed of physical matter and form or essential parts — for only of those is it true that when one is destroyed the other can remain in actual existence.

7. Sixth: if the spiritual seed converts into a soul, generation cannot occur without the seed's perishing; yet the seed's form (the soul) would remain, and substantial conversion requires the prior form's perishing. So Bright's opinion is no safer than the preceding.
source_text:
ART. XIV.
Confutatur quinta sententia, quae est Timothei Bright Cantabrigiensis.

1. Cum extremam manum huic disputationi admovebam, cum acutissimi Timothei Brighti Cantabrigiensis librum de Sanitate, de Morbo, & de Morte, in manus meas incidit; in quo ille novam & insolitam sententiam de origine animae proponit. Verba ejus haec sunt: Quibus respondemus, nec totam, nec partem animi parentum traduci, neque accidens aliquod animi rudimentum esse. Quid ergo? Sane substantiam quandam ab anima natam, nec totam ipsam nec partem, tanquam animae immortale semen, prolis animae futurae principium: & sicut semen corporeum de parentum corporibus decisum nec corpus ipsum, nec corporis aliquod membrum emittit, ita anima per semen animae fecundum, non per animam aut animae partem aliquam, traducitur in prolem: & paulo post, Ergo tenemus, animam ut integram & absolutam parentibus referendam acceptam; sed seminale quid ab anima, aeque atque a corpore exclusum, & tandem verbi illius virtute (sc. foecunditatis benedictione) in animam rationalem & immortalem proditurum.

2. Hanc sententiam clarissimi & doctissimi Timothei sic confuto. Primo: Spiritus ille seu semen spirituale, quod a parentis anima excluditur & emittitur, vere & realiter praeexistebat in anima: realis enim emissio praesupponit reale inesse; at spiritus ille non potest realiter inesse animae parentis: Ergo neque realiter excludi & emitti ab ea. Probatur assumptio: spiritus ille non potest inesse animae patris ut pars in toto, fatente ipso Timotheo; neque ut accidens in subjecto, idque quia est substantia; substantiae autem repugnat inesse subjecto; neque ut res in loco ambiente, aut in vase continente — talis enim modus continentiae & circumscriptionis naturae spirituali animae repugnat.

3. Secundo: semen illud spirituale vel fit ex tota anima patris, vel ex parte animae patris, vel ex nihilo: non enim potest fieri ex materia corporea, tum quia est spiritualis substantia, tum quia ipse Brightus testatur illud non ex corpore sed ex anima natum esse: non fit ex tota anima patris, quia sic anima patris tota in semen converteretur; non ex parte, quia anima est indivisibilis; Ergo ex nihilo — quod creationem importat.

4. Tertio: conversio illius seminis spiritualis in animam vel est conversio accidentalis, qualis est conversio seu mutatio qua homo malus convertitur & mutatur in bonum, & color albus in nigrum; vel est conversio substantialis, qualis fuit conversio uxoris Loth in statuam salis, & conversio ligni in substantiam illius ignis cui approximatur. Non est conversio accidentalis, quia inde sequeretur semen illud spirituale non differre specie & essentialiter, sed gradu perfectionis accidentalis, ab anima — hoc est, esse animam rationalem accidentali aliqua ratione inchoatam & imperfectam: hoc autem contradicit verbis ipsius Timothei, dicentis semen illud non esse actu animam sed animae futurae principium. Si vero est conversio substantialis, tunc vel fit per abolitionem totius, vel per abolitionem unius partis essentiae altera remanente.

5. Quarto: DEUS valeat semen illud annihilare, & eo annihilato animam eodem instanti ex nihilo producere; non patri sed DEO soli tunc animae productio adscribenda est — quod ingens absurdum est, si vera sit ipsorum doctrina de traduce.

6. Quinto: conversio seminis in animam non potest fieri per abolitionem unius partis essentiae, altera remanente: primo, quia inde sequeretur spiritualem substantiam seminis illius esse corruptibilem & capacem transmutationis substantialis, non minus quam corpora Physica; illa enim aboleri & destrui possunt naturaliter quoad unam solam essentiae partem, formam videlicet: secundo, sequeretur substantiam illam spiritualem esse compositam ex materia & forma Physica, aut in partes essentiales — nam de his solis verum est quod earum una destructa altera remanere possit superstes quoad actualem existentiam.

7. Sexto: generationem hominis fieri sine interitu seminis non potest, si semen illud spirituale in animam convertitur; forma enim seminis, i.e. anima, maneret — at conversio substantialis interitum prioris formae requirit. Unde concludo Brighti sententiam non magis tutam esse quam praecedentes.
